title: Economics Basics Diagnostic Assessment
description: These 12 questions check the starting ideas behind all nine ECONOVA courses: scarcity and opportunity cost, markets and prices, market failure, the whole economy, income, taxes and money, trade, and reasoning about SDG policy evidence. You do not need to have studied economics before. Scoring follows fixed rules only (no AI grading), and the result is only a suggestion to help you choose a difficulty level.

review.note: AI-written question draft (v3 redesign: covers foundational ideas from c01-c09, one question per concept area plus two SDG reasoning questions; written for students before instruction). Not yet reviewed by a teacher; the difficulty thresholds are provisional and have not been validated.

thresholds.note: Below 40% correct suggests beginner, 40% to under 75% suggests intermediate, and 75% or higher suggests advanced. These are provisional thresholds that have not been validated with student data.

market_ceiling.title: A market with a legal maximum price
market_ceiling.caption: A hypothetical market. The vertical axis shows price, the horizontal axis shows quantity, and the dashed line is the maximum price set by the government.

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A town owns one empty lot. It could turn the lot into a park, a parking lot, or a community garden. Residents value the park most, the parking lot second, and the garden third, so the town builds the park. What is the opportunity cost of building the park?

choices.text: The enjoyment residents will get from the new park
The parking lot and the garden added together
The parking lot, the next-best use of the land
The garden, the use residents value the least

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A popular video convinces many people that oat milk is healthy, so they want to buy more of it at every price. Nothing changes for the farms and firms that make oat milk. What most likely happens to the price of oat milk and the quantity sold?

choices.text: The price rises, and the quantity sold rises
The price rises, and the quantity sold falls
The price falls, and the quantity sold rises
The price falls, and the quantity sold falls

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: The graph shows a market for one good. The government then sets a legal maximum price (a price ceiling), shown by the dashed line. At that maximum price, what happens?

choices.text: Sellers offer more than buyers want, so there is a surplus
Buyers want more than sellers offer, so there is a shortage
Buyers and sellers want the same amount, so the market clears
Buyers want less of the good, so the demand curve shifts left

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A paint factory pays for its workers, materials, and electricity, but it pays nothing for the smoke that makes nearby residents sick. If no rule or fee changes this, how does the amount of paint produced compare with the amount that would be best for society as a whole?

choices.text: It is about right, because buyers pay the market price
It is too low, because the factory sells paint below cost
It is too low, because sick residents buy less paint
It is too high, because the factory ignores the harm

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A neighborhood has no streetlights. Every household would benefit from them, and once the lights are on, no one can be stopped from enjoying them. A company offers to install the lights if households pay for them voluntarily. What is the most likely problem?

choices.text: The light gets used up as more households use it
Many hope others will pay, so too little is raised
The company earns large profits from selling the lights
Households compete to pay first, so too many are built

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: This year, the total dollar value of everything a country produced rose by 10%. Over the same year, the prices of the goods and services it produced also rose by about 10% on average. What most likely happened to the actual amount of goods and services produced?

choices.text: It rose by about 10%, the same as the dollar value
It rose by about 20%, adding both increases together
It stayed about the same, as prices explain the rise
It fell by about 10%, since prices went up by 10%

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A town has 1,000 adults. Of these, 360 have jobs, 40 have no job but are actively looking for one, and 600 are not looking for work (for example, full-time students and retirees). Economists count the people who have a job or are actively looking for one as the labor force. What percentage of the labor force is unemployed? Enter a number in percent, rounded to the nearest whole percent (for example, 7).

Hypothetical example: Under a new tax, Lee earns $20,000 a year and pays $2,000 in tax, while Kim earns $80,000 a year and pays $16,000 in tax. Compared with Lee, what share of income does Kim pay in tax?

choices.text: A larger share of income than Lee pays
The same share of income as Lee pays
A smaller share of income than Lee pays
A share that these numbers cannot show

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: You put $500 in a savings account that pays 10% interest per year. Each year's interest is added to the balance, and the next year's interest is paid on the new balance. You make no other deposits or withdrawals. What is the balance after 2 years? Enter a number in dollars, rounded to the nearest whole dollar. Round only at the final step.

Hypothetical example: In one hour, Ana can bake 6 cakes or sew 3 shirts. In one hour, Ben can bake 4 cakes or sew 1 shirt. They want to split the work and trade so that, together, they give up as few cakes as possible for the shirts they make. Who should sew the shirts, and why?

choices.text: Ben, because he gives up fewer cakes per shirt
Ben, because Ana is faster and should bake instead
Ana should do both tasks, since she is faster at each
Ana, because each shirt costs her fewer cakes

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: In a rural district, many children miss morning classes. A survey finds that most of these children spend early mornings walking to a distant well to collect water for their families. A student is defining this problem for an SDG project. Which of these is most likely a root cause rather than a symptom?

choices.text: The hours children spend fetching water far away
The empty seats teachers notice in morning classes
The low attendance numbers in the district's records
The lower test scores of children who miss classes

questions.prompt: Hypothetical example: A city made its buses free for one year. Officials claim that the free buses reduced car traffic. Which piece of evidence would best support their claim?

choices.text: A survey in which most riders said they like free buses
Traffic fell in a year when gas prices also rose sharply
Car trips fell more than in a similar city with paid buses
The city spent more on its bus service than it had planned
